claims.claim: Refused Constantius's demand to condemn Athanasius: "My standing alone does not make the truth a whit the weaker"; "Neither three days nor three months can change my sentiments"
claims.witness: A record copied by Theodoret, Church History II.13 (npnf203 l.9655-9659, 9749, 9829-9830)

claims.claim: Banished to Beroea in Thrace; returned the emperor's gold, "he has need of them to pay his troops"
Taken from Rome by night for fear of the people
Gave way after two years and subscribed from fear of death
claims.witness: Athanasius, History of the Arians 41 (npnf204 l.39175-39177), an ally

claims.claim: Worn out by exile, signed heresy and entered Rome as a victor; urged by Fortunatianus
Signed a Sirmium creed with his own statement
The letters of his lapse are doubtful
The crowd cried "One God, one Christ, one bishop"; Liberius returned and Felix withdrew
Died on 24 September, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus
claims.witness: Gesta inter Liberium et Felicem (Collectio Avellana l.5098-5099); Hartranft's year 366 (npnf202 l.38766)

claims.claim: Gave the veil to Ambrose's sister at Christmas in Saint Peter's: "You, my daughter, have desired a good espousal"
claims.witness: Ambrose, On Virgins III (npnf210 l.38125-38137), as Ambrose recalls it

contested_claims.claim: Whether and how he lapsed in exile
contested_claims.sides: Athanasius: signed from fear of death, forced (npnf204 l.39175-39177). Jerome: worn out, signed heresy (Chronicle l.45536-45540; Lives 97). Sozomen: signed at Sirmium with his own statement (npnf202 l.33576-33583). Theodoret: no lapse told. Feder: the fall letters doubtful (l.15187).
Socrates: the party of Ursacius (npnf202 l.8934). Jerome: Acacius (npnf203 l.41312). Book of the Popes: Liberius himself, an account Loomis calls a medley of fact and legend.

absent_details.detail: Birth, family and career before his election
absent_details.note: Only the late Book of the Popes gives a father's name; no early source used here gives them.

claims.claim: Wrote to Julius from Rome after a year and three months there, in his own hand, with his creed; said he had refuted the Arians at Nicaea; confessed the Word always co-existing with the Father and a kingdom without end
Wrote against Asterius and fell into the error of Paul of Samosata, that Christ was a mere man
Taught that the Son began when born of Mary and that his kingdom would end; deposed at Constantinople, Basil installed
Some held he had only propounded questions, misconstrued by his enemies
Cleared by Julius and the Western bishops at Sardica
claims.witness: Julius and the Council of Sardica, quoted by Athanasius (npnf204 l.23394, 24186-24193)

claims.claim: "The most execrable of all heretics"
claims.witness: The Eastern bishops' letter, quoted in Zenos's note (npnf202 l.6704-6708); hostile

claims.claim: Athanasius only smiled when asked about him
Athanasius refused him communion
claims.witness: Hilary's dossier (l.12874); denied by Watson (npnf209 l.4343-4344)

claims.claim: Died about two years before Epiphanius wrote
The Marcellians condemned in canon 1 of Constantinople 381; Marcellus himself afterwards acknowledged the truth
claims.witness: Canon 1 (npnf214 l.13975); Hefele as quoted by Percival (l.14004-14007)

contested_claims.sides: Julius and the Western bishops at Sardica: cleared (npnf204 l.23394, 24193). The Eastern bishops, Socrates's and Sozomen's accounts of the charges, and Basil (npnf208 l.43341-43343): condemned. Epiphanius: left to God (PG42 l.28684).
Epiphanius: Athanasius only smiled, and treated him as cleared (PG42 l.29108). Hilary's dossier: refused him communion (l.12874). Watson: he never did so (npnf209 l.4343-4344).

contested_claims.claim: Whether he returned to the truth
contested_claims.sides: Hefele, quoted by Percival: yes (npnf214 l.14004-14007). The Benedictine note to Basil: he seems to have erred at the end (npnf208 l.43542).

absent_details.detail: Birth, family, and when he became bishop

absent_details.note: Neither is held; the book is known through opponents and the Sardica letter.

claims.claim: Tied four robbers together and carried them to the church, asking "what do you bid me do with these?"; they too left the world
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 19 (l.335); a book of holy lives

claims.claim: An Ethiopian, black, a house-servant driven out by his master for immorality and brigandage; said to have led a robber band and murdered
Gave himself up to a monastery after one of his adventures
Tempted by demons toward lust; stood praying at night for six years; answered Isidore "I will never cease until the appearance of the demons ceases"
Died at Scete aged seventy-five, a priest, leaving seventy disciples
claims.witness: Palladius (l.337); Sozomen VI.29 (npnf202 l.39499-39525), following Palladius

claims.claim: "An Egyptian"
Driven from the sanctuary by the clergy to test him, "Get outside, O Ethiopian"; answered himself "They have treated thee rightly"
claims.witness: Syriac sayings, Budge vol. II (l.1028); the saying names him "Abba Moses" and the clergy "Ethiopian"

claims.claim: Killed by barbarians at Scete with seven brothers
The Moses of the sayings is the robber

contested_claims.sides: Palladius: "an Ethiopian by race and black" (l.333). Sozomen: "Moses, an Egyptian" (npnf202 l.39461).

Palladius and Sozomen: died at Scete at seventy-five, with no violence told. A Syriac saying: an Abba Moses killed by barbarians with seven brothers (Budge vol. II l.1464), not named as the Ethiopian.

contested_claims.claim: Whether Cassian's Abbot Moses is the same man
contested_claims.sides: Cassian's Moses spent his boyhood near Antony (npnf211 l.27198-27199). Gibson: probably another, possibly Moses the Libyan (npnf211 l.24272-24276).

absent_details.detail: Years of birth and death; family; his master's name; his ordaining bishop
absent_details.note: No held line gives them; Palladius gives only his age at death.
None; his words survive only in Palladius and in collected sayings.

claims.claim: Led the newly baptized British army against Saxons and Picts; the bishops shouted Alleluia three times and the enemy fled
claims.witness: Constantius, Life (l.2993-3073); hagiography; Levison knows no other record of the raid (l.3026)

claims.claim: Constantius wrote about 480 or a little after
Born at Auxerre of noble parents; studied law at Rome; pleaded in the prefect's courts; married; made governor of provinces
Demanded as bishop by clergy and people with one voice; took the office unwilling
Pope Celestine, urged by the deacon Palladius, sent him against the Pelagian Agricola in Britain
claims.witness: Prosper's Chronicle (Mommsen l.54151-54155); the year 429 is Mommsen's

claims.claim: A large synod of Gallic bishops chose Germanus and Lupus after an embassy from Britain
A second journey with a bishop named Severus
Bede copied Constantius almost word for word for the British chapters
Went to Ravenna, where Placidia ruled with Valentinian; asked that his body be sent home, which she granted unwillingly; died on the seventh day of his illness
Died after 444, on 31 July
Famous for miracles and strictness of life

contested_claims.sides: Prosper: Pope Celestine, at the urging of the deacon Palladius (Mommsen l.54151-54155). Constantius, with Bede after him: a Gallic synod, after an embassy from Britain (l.2664-2670). Levison: attempts to join them are "merae coniecturae" (l.193-194).

absent_details.detail: Birth year, his wife's name in an early source, writings
absent_details.note: Constantius gives no year and no name; Levison reports the wife's name only from the later Gesta of Auxerre; no writing of his is held.

claims.claim: Hurried on foot into Rome without horse or pack animal after Celidonius appealed; told Leo he came for courtesy, not for a case
claims.witness: Life of Hilary, extract in Mansi VI (l.44880-44901); partisan, authorship doubted by the editors (l.44827-44829)

claims.claim: Celidonius proved he was wrongly deposed; Hilary used words no layman could make and no priest listen to; travelled like a courier, with soldiers; lost his power over the province of Vienne
Leo's "not very creditable encounter with Hilary"
Of noble birth and very differently brought up; chose poverty and farmed beyond his strength
Honoratus came back to their homeland for his sake; he resisted; then thanked Jesus who broke his chains
Succeeded Honoratus as bishop of Arles
Kinsman of Honoratus
claims.witness: His own words, "sicut sanguinis sui venam" (PL50 l.1811-1812), with the editors' chapter head (l.1778)

claims.claim: A fiery torrent of faith and heavenly eloquence
claims.witness: Constantius, Life of Germanus (constantius-lyon file l.3376-3378)

claims.claim: Dead by 22 August 449
claims.witness: Leo, Letter 40 (npnf212 l.6513-6528); the year is Feltoe's from the consuls

contested_claims.sides: Life of Hilary: the charge was confirmed by witnesses (Mansi l.44883-44884). Leo: he proved himself wrongly deposed (npnf212 l.2163-2166).
Richardson: about 401 (npnf203 l.43388). Jackson: he died at forty-one in 449 (npnf203 l.3089-3090).

absent_details.detail: Birthplace, parents, and the year of his turning

absent_details.note: Held only as the extract quoted in Mansi VI.

claims.claim: In 429 gave a Commonitorium in Greek on Caelestius to the church of Constantinople, offered to the emperor Theodosius; Caelestius and Julian were then driven from the city and later condemned at Ephesus
claims.witness: The work's title, quoted by Garnier (PL48 l.396-403); the year from its consuls, Garnier (l.404)

claims.claim: Caelestius a follower of Pelagius
Not named by Gennadius
Augustine wrote to him as son, received his letters at Carthage, and had not known how far he had progressed
Origin: southern Italy or Africa
A layman
Translated sermons of Nestorius with letters of Nestorius and Cyril, so that Latin readers might know and avoid them
claims.witness: His preface (PL48 l.58505-58515); dated after Ephesus by Garnier's note

claims.claim: Nestorius's twelve anathemas survive only in his Latin
Traced the error back to Theodore of Mopsuestia in his book against Julian
claims.witness: Preface to the Liber Subnotationum (PL48 l.6828-6844); partisan

claims.claim: Translated word for word so as not to be proved a forger

contested_claims.sides: Garnier: Campania, Apulia or southern Italy (PL48 l.459-462). Baluze: Africa (l.2220-2224). Schoenemann: both rest on conjecture (l.2290-2296). Warfield: an African layman (npnf105 l.1468).
Garnier: he did not reach it, or wrote nothing after it (as Baluze reports, l.2262-2266). Baluze: he outlived it, since he names the Eutychians (l.2266-2273).

absent_details.note: No ancient line gives them; his lay status is an editors' inference.

claims.claim: "I confess that our LORD was of Two Natures before the Union, but after the Union I confess Him to be of One Nature"
claims.witness: Minutes of Flavian's synod, read at Ephesus 449 (Perry l.23843-23845); Leo's Tome quotes it (npnf212 l.5597)

claims.claim: Accused by Eusebius of Dorylaeum and deposed by Flavian
claims.witness: Eutyches to Leo (npnf212 l.4518-4520); Flavian's sentence (Perry l.23980-23981)

claims.claim: The synod met in November 448
Dedicated to God at birth; spent seventy years in continence
claims.witness: His petition (Perry l.23388-23390); his letter to Leo (npnf212 l.4605)

claims.claim: Took refuge with Leo, anathematizing Apollinaris, Nestorius and other heretics; "I stand in jeopardy of my life as a heretic"
Said the minutes were falsified
Basil of Seleucia denied a sentence; Juvenal: "This sentence, therefore, was altered"
Appealed to Rome at the trial
Restored "to his Monastery and to his Grade" at Ephesus 449
"Very unwary and exceedingly ignorant"
Chalcedon received the Tome "for the removal of the false doctrines of Eutyches"
Leo urged that he be banished further
claims.witness: Feltoe's summary of an untranslated letter (npnf212 l.11331-11333)

claims.claim: Chalcedon "introduced and increased the heresy of Nestorius", yet Eutyches "affirmed an inaccurate dogma"
claims.witness: Chronicle of Zachariah of Mitylene, so called (l.2174-2178, 1168-1172)

claims.claim: Chrysaphius was his godson
claims.witness: Liberatus, Breviarium 11 (PL68 l.78115-78118, rough OCR); Feltoe (npnf212 l.588-589)

contested_claims.claim: Whether the minutes of 448 were true
contested_claims.sides: Eutyches: what he said was not written, and what he did not say was (Perry l.23308-23311). At Ephesus 449 Basil of Seleucia denied a sentence, and Juvenal said it was altered (l.23864-23873). Flavian's synod and Leo rely on them.
Eutyches: he lodged a writ of appeal (npnf212 l.4527). Flavian: "this he certainly never did" (l.5023).

absent_details.detail: Birth, death, family, and the name of his monastery
absent_details.note: No held line gives them; his age rests on his own "seventy years".

claims.claim: Wrote to Augustine that they had exchanged letters through the deacon Leontius, and that many servants of Christ at Marseilles thought his teaching on the calling of the elect went against the Fathers
claims.witness: His letter, Augustine Ep. 225 (PL33 l.73494-73525); partisan on the Massilians

claims.claim: A man of Aquitaine, "scholastic in style and vigorous in statement"
A layman
claims.witness: Gibson (npnf211 l.15695); Garnier (PL48 l.571); against: Mommsen (l.42769-42771)

claims.claim: The letter to Augustine dates to 429
claims.witness: Gibson, from Hilary's recent succession at Arles (npnf211 l.15720-15721)

claims.claim: Wrote the poem On the Ungrateful after Augustine's replies
With the layman Hilary, appealed to Pope Celestine and won a letter to the bishops of Gaul
Wrote an unsigned book against works of Cassian
claims.witness: Gennadius, who sided with Cassian (npnf203 l.43667-43671); Gibson (npnf211 l.15770-15772)

claims.claim: His chronicle ran to the Vandal capture of Rome
Pope Celestine, urged by the deacon Palladius, sent Germanus of Auxerre against the Pelagians in Britain
claims.witness: Prosper's Chronicle (Mommsen l.54151-54155), the year 429 being Mommsen's

claims.claim: Letters of Leo against Eutyches were thought to have been dictated by him
claims.witness: Gennadius (npnf203 l.43672-43675), with the variant "said" in Richardson's note

claims.claim: Gennadius's account does not show that he left Gaul; the notary of the Roman church is a medieval inference
Augustine died during the Vandal siege, answering Julian's books and defending the grace of Christ
claims.witness: Prosper's Chronicle (Mommsen l.54206-54209); Julian named "Aeclanensis" by Prosper at l.54540

contested_claims.sides: Gibson, "also a layman" (npnf211 l.15695), and Garnier (PL48 l.571): yes. Mommsen: a cleric when he wrote to Augustine, since he calls the deacon Leontius his brother (l.42769-42771).

Gennadius: Leo's letters against Eutyches "are also thought" to have been dictated by him (some manuscripts "said"). Medieval writers: a notary of the Roman church. Mommsen: the account does not show he even left Gaul (l.42790-42793).

absent_details.note: No ancient source used here gives them. Mommsen: his city is unknown (l.42726-42727), and he lived at least to 455 (l.42793-42794). The years 403 to 463 are Richardson's note (npnf203 l.43663) and Freese's note to Photius (l.3543).

absent_details.detail: His books against Cassian and On the Ungrateful
absent_details.note: Not held, except one verse of On the Ungrateful quoted in a note to Leo's letters.

claims.claim: Retold the magi's story of Zurvan's sacrifice and doubt, Ormizd and Ahriman, and refuted it
claims.witness: Refutation of the Sects II, extract (Langlois l.49638-49649, 49828-49842); a polemicist on an opposing faith

claims.claim: Pupil of Sahak and Mesrop, sent with Joseph to Edessa to translate the Scriptures from Syriac, then to Constantinople; joined there by Leon and Koriun; returned with the Scriptures and the canons of Nicaea and Ephesus
Went to Byzantium without orders, misled by lying letters
Translations made from the copies were found faulty
Bishop of Bagrevand among the bishops at Artashat who answered the edict of Mihr-Nerseh
claims.witness: Elishe (Langlois l.27326-27354; edict l.27118-27129); Lazar of Pharp (l.38316-38342, OCR "Emig")

claims.claim: No biographer recorded his birth or death
claims.witness: Introduction to the Refutation in Langlois's collection (l.49402-49405)

claims.claim: One of the most famous Armenian writers of the fifth century

contested_claims.sides: Koriun: Sahak and Mesrop sent him to Edessa, and he went on to Byzantium to study (Langlois l.3807-3849). Moses of Khoren: lying letters drew him there without his teachers' order (l.24619-24622).

absent_details.detail: Birth, death, and the date of his book
absent_details.note: The introduction in Langlois's collection says no one recorded his birth or death (l.49402-49405); no held line dates the Refutation or the assembly at Artashat.
Only part of book II is held, in French (Langlois l.49545-49550).
